target.title: Divine Hiddenness, Greater Goods, and Accommodation
target.thesis: Valuable goods made sufficiently more valuable by divine hiddenness can give God a sufficient reason to remain hidden, so nonresistant nonbelief does not entail that God does not exist.

W2575351351.c001.text: If God exists, every nonresistant creature capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God is able to participate in that relationship merely by trying.
W2575351351.c001.quote: Necessarily, if God exists, anyone who is (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God is also (iii) in a position to participate in such relationship (able to do so just by trying).

W2575351351.c002.text: A person can participate in meaningful conscious relationship with God at a time only if that person believes that God exists at that time.
W2575351351.c002.quote: Necessarily, one is at a time in a position to participate in meaningful conscious relationship with God only if at that time one believes that God exists.

W2575351351.c003.text: If God exists, every nonresistant creature capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God believes that God exists.
W2575351351.c003.quote: Necessarily, if God exists, anyone who is (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God also (iii) believes that God exists [from (1) and (2)].

W2575351351.c004.text: Some people are nonresistant and capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God but do not believe that God exists.
W2575351351.c004.quote: There are (and often have been) people who are (i) not resisting God and (ii) capable of meaningful conscious relationship with God without also (iii) believing that God exists.

W2575351351.c006.text: The inference from the claim about nonresistant believers and the existence of nonresistant nonbelievers to God's nonexistence is valid.
W2575351351.c006.quote: The inference from (3) and (4) to (5) is valid, and so one must deny one of these premises in order to maintain that God exists.

W2575351351.c007.text: A perfectly loving God would desire the highest well-being of creatures, which for creatures able to relate personally to God includes a personal relationship with God.
W2575351351.c007.quote: Early on, Schellenberg supported premise (1) by arguing that if a perfectly loving God were to exist, He would desire the highest well-being for His creatures. For all creatures that are capable of personally relating to God, their highest well-being would include a personal relationship with Him.

W2575351351.c008.text: If a person would be better off temporarily not knowing that God exists, an omnibenevolent God would not reveal Godself to that person during that time.
W2575351351.c008.quote: It seems clear that if some person were better off not knowing that God exists (at least for a time), God would not reveal Himself to that person (at that time) even though He desires a personal relationship with that person for its own sake.

W2575351351.c009.text: Greater-goods responses contend that an all-loving God can desire the best for creatures while allowing nonresistant nonbelief for the sake of a greater good.
W2575351351.c009.quote: Greater goods style responses address the support for premise (1) by attempting to demonstrate that an all-loving God could consistently desire the best for His creatures while simultaneously allowing them to be nonresistant nonbelievers.

W2575351351.c010.text: Schellenberg's accommodation strategy holds that a proposed good cannot justify nonresistant nonbelief if God could obtain that good within a personal relationship with God.
W2575351351.c010.quote: If this can be shown, then these goods cannot count as a sufficient reason for God to allow nonresistant nonbelief.

W2575351351.c011.text: God may reasonably permit nonresistant nonbelief when doing so is no worse than another way of obtaining a significantly greater good.
W2575351351.c011.quote: But Daniel Howard-Snyder (1996) points out, ‘if permitting [nonresistant] nonbelief is no worse than any other means for some significantly greater good to obtain’, then God might reasonably allow for nonresistant nonbelief to obtain in order to acquire that greater good.

W2575351351.c012.text: A good may overcome the accommodation strategy if temporary nonresistant nonbelief makes that good sufficiently more valuable.
W2575351351.c012.quote: I suggest that a proposed good might overcome the accommodation strategy if that good is somehow more valuable given temporary nonresistant nonbelief. If nonresistant nonbelief sufficiently increases the value of some good, then it will constitute a sufficient reason for God to allow for nonresistant nonbelief.

W2575351351.c013.text: The many-goods response holds that multiple goods jointly produced by nonresistant nonbelief can provide God sufficient reason to allow it, even if no single good can.
W2575351351.c013.quote: Rather than identifying a single good as a proposed reason for why God might allow for nonresistant nonbelief, the ‘many goods’ response [MGR] admits that no single good may be sufficient. Instead, the MGR holds that the multitude of goods brought about by nonresistant nonbelief together provide a sufficient reason for God to allow for nonresistant nonbelief.

W2575351351.c014.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.
W2575351351.c014.quote: This is because nonresistant nonbelief is a single evil (if it can be properly called an evil), and multiple goods may arise from a single instance of evil without that evil increasing.

W2575351351.c015.text: If a world containing nonresistant nonbelief has greater total value than a relevantly comparable world without it, God has sufficient reason to create the former.
W2575351351.c015.quote: If W has a total value which is greater than W′, then God has a sufficient reason to bring about W rather than W′.

W2575351351.c016.text: Refuting one proposed good does not refute the many-goods response to divine hiddenness.
W2575351351.c016.quote: Even if a critic is able to demonstrate that some particular good does not qualify as contributing to the overall value brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, she will not have demonstrated that the MGR fails.

W2575351351.c017.text: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God can collectively make a world containing nonresistant nonbelief more valuable.
W2575351351.c017.quote: Any good at all that is brought about by nonresistant nonbelief will contribute to the overall value of W. This means that the task of identifying goods might actually be relatively simple.

W2575351351.c018.text: The many-goods response can succeed even when nonresistant nonbelief is not logically necessary for any individual good.
W2575351351.c018.quote: Even if for each good identified for the MGR there is some possible way to attain that good without allowing for nonresistant nonbelief, the MGR may still succeed.

W2575351351.c019.text: The many-goods response succeeds if nonresistant nonbelief is the only way for God to obtain enough goods, or if alternatives cause more evil.
W2575351351.c019.quote: So long as nonresistant nonbelief is the only way for God to acquire a sufficient number of goods, the MGR will succeed. The MGR will also succeed if all of the goods in question might be acquired by some means other than nonresistant nonbelief, but that other means causes a greater amount of evil than nonresistant nonbelief.

W2575351351.c020.text: Schellenberg’s accommodation strategy does not defeat the many-goods response merely because an individual good can occur within a relationship with God.
W2575351351.c020.quote: But the accommodation strategy is not so devastating against the MGR. Even if some particular good might be possible to acquire within a relationship with God, it might still count in favour of W, rather than W′.

W2575351351.c021.text: The many-goods response may succeed even if every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God.
W2575351351.c021.quote: Given this, it is possible that the MGR will succeed even if every good identified can also be realized within a relationship with God.

W2575351351.c022.text: If the comparative values of worlds with and without nonresistant nonbelief are too close to determine, the argument from divine hiddenness reaches a stalemate.
W2575351351.c022.quote: If this is the case, then argument from divine hiddenness will result in a stalemate.

W2575351351.c023.text: A relationship with God may be infinitely valuable, or so valuable that no collection of other goods can outweigh its loss.
W2575351351.c023.quote: A proponent of the Problem of Divine Hiddenness might argue that the value of a relationship with God is so great that the total value necessary to outweigh it cannot be achieved even by a great number of other goods.

W2575351351.c024.text: A relationship between God and an imperfect human is reasonably regarded as finitely valuable.
W2575351351.c024.quote: It is reasonable to suppose that a relationship between God and a human would be of finite value on account of the human’s imperfection.

W2575351351.c025.text: Even if a relationship with God is not infinitely valuable, goods arising from nonresistant nonbelief may be unable to outweigh its value.
W2575351351.c025.quote: Even if the value of a relationship with God is not infinite, it might still be so great that there simply aren’t enough goods from nonresistant nonbelief to outweigh the value of a relationship with God.

W2575351351.c026.text: Temporary nonresistant nonbelief can be followed by a person's choice to enter a relationship with God, whereas permanent nonresistant nonbelief cannot.
W2575351351.c026.quote: Temporary nonresistant nonbelief allows for the possibility that the person in question might eventually choose to enter into a relationship with God, while permanent nonresistant nonbelief does not allow for this.

W2575351351.c027.text: Permanent nonresistant nonbelief prevents a person from ever entering a relationship with God.
W2575351351.c027.quote: If some person is a permanent nonresistant nonbeliever, then she can never enter into a relationship with God.

W2575351351.c028.text: For permanent nonresistant nonbelief, the lost value of a relationship with God is plausibly too great for the resulting goods to outweigh.
W2575351351.c028.quote: It is reasonable to think that in this case the value of the relationship lost would be so great that the goods gained from the individual’s nonresistant nonbelief would be insufficient to outweigh that lost value.

W2575351351.c029.text: When nonresistant nonbelief is temporary and followed by a relationship with God, its lost value may be outweighed by many goods.
W2575351351.c029.quote: If she does enter into a relationship with God sometime after she comes to believe, then it seems reasonable that that the total value lost by her temporary nonresistant nonbelief would not be so great that it could not be outweighed by many goods.

W2575351351.c030.text: A world containing temporary nonresistant nonbelief may have greater total value than an alternative world without it.
W2575351351.c030.quote: That is, the total value of W might still be greater than the total value of W′ if the nonresistant nonbelief within W is temporary.

W2575351351.c031.text: It is not evident that permanent nonresistant nonbelief occurs, because people who die as nonbelievers may become believers after death.
W2575351351.c031.quote: But unlike temporary nonresistant nonbelief, it is not obvious that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually occurs. Even if many nonresistant nonbelievers die without deathbed conversions, they may become postmortem believers.

W2575351351.c032.text: Without evidence that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually or probably occurs, its incompatibility with God does not threaten theism.
W2575351351.c032.quote: So unless one can demonstrate that permanent nonresistant nonbelief actually occurs, or very likely occurs, the mere fact that it is incompatible with the existence of God does not pose a threat to theism.

W2575351351.c033.text: Permanent nonresistant nonbelief cannot independently support atheism because evidence for or against it depends on whether atheism or theism is probable.
W2575351351.c033.quote: Thus, we should remain agnostic about the existence of permanent nonresistant nonbelievers until we determine whether atheism or theism is very probable. But this means that we cannot use the existence of permanent nonresistant nonbelief in an independent argument for atheism.

W2575351351.c034.text: All possible worlds are comparable in value.
W2575351351.c034.quote: I move forward on the assumption that all worlds are comparable.

W2575351351.c035.text: Human inability to make accurate value judgments does not show that an omniscient being cannot compare possible worlds.
W2575351351.c035.quote: For it may be that any reason to think that they are not comparable proves only that humans are incapable of making accurate judgments of value. But this does not mean that an omniscient being would be incapable of making such judgments.

W2575351351.c036.text: The MGR assumes that God can know all the relevant details and values of possible worlds before creating one.
W2575351351.c036.quote: their values, He must know what those values are prior to creating.

W2575351351.c037.text: Whether God can know every detail of a world containing libertarian free will before creating it is controversial.
W2575351351.c037.quote: But whether God can know all the minute details of the world He creates—especially if that world includes creaturely libertarian free will—is controversial.

W2575351351.c038.text: The MGR would be stronger if it did not depend on a controversial doctrine about divine foreknowledge.
W2575351351.c038.quote: It would be a virtue for the success of the MGR not to depend on the truth of a controversial position like this.

W2575351351.c039.text: Even if open theism is true, God might judge that the potential goods enabled by nonresistant nonbelief outweigh its potential risks.
W2575351351.c039.quote: As long as God knows that there are many goods which can come about only given nonresistant nonbelief, He might be able to determine that the potential reward is greater than the potential risk.

W2575351351.c040.text: If nonresistant nonbelief produces many goods, theism must explain why God permits so many believers rather than universal nonresistant nonbelief.
W2575351351.c040.quote: If there are many goods that are brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, then why is the number of believers so high? Why doesn’t God desire for there to be universal nonresistant nonbelief?

W2575351351.c041.text: God may sacrifice a relationship only when several goods together are sufficiently valuable, and some of those goods may require believers.
W2575351351.c041.quote: First, since no single good is valuable enough on its own for God to sacrifice the good of a relationship, God could only justify sacrificing a relationship with a person if it would allow for a number of goods which together were sufficiently valuable. Second, many of the goods might be possible only if some believers exist.

W2575351351.c042.text: Nonresistant nonbelief may enable morally significant free choices because awareness of God can make choosing rightly easier.
W2575351351.c042.quote: God would make Himself hidden so that humans could have a real opportunity to exercise their will.

W2575351351.c043.text: Some morally significant choices are more valuable and require greater strength of will when made by nonresistant nonbelievers than by believers.
W2575351351.c043.quote: It seems plausible that there are at least some cases in which a morally significant free choice is more valuable, and in which choosing the good demonstrates a greater strength of will, when it is chosen by a person who does not even have evidence sufficient for belief in the existence of God.

W2575351351.c044.text: Allowing nonresistant nonbelief lets some humans bear the responsibility of telling others that God exists.
W2575351351.c044.quote: A second benefit of allowing for nonresistant nonbelief is that it makes it possible for some humans to have the responsibility of telling other humans about God’s existence.

W2575351351.c045.text: God may temporarily remain hidden until a person is prepared to seek a relationship with God for the right reasons.
W2575351351.c045.quote: God might remain hidden from someone until she is ready to respond in the right way.

W2575351351.c046.text: Nonresistant nonbelief can make genuine self-sacrifice possible because a person who believes no God exists can give up life without hope of an afterlife.
W2575351351.c046.quote: But unless she sacrifices her life knowing that she is truly giving everything up, her sacrifice cannot be genuine.

W2575351351.c047.text: World W permits a greater variety of personal testimonies about entering a relationship with God than world W′.
W2575351351.c047.quote: In W, there can be a greater variety of personal testimony about entering into a relationship with God.

W2575351351.c048.text: Personal testimonies can be good for both the person giving the testimony and the community that receives it.
W2575351351.c048.quote: It is plausible that an individual’s personal testimony can be good for both the individual and for the community to which an individual shares her testimony.

W2575351351.c049.text: A person's story of entering a relationship with God may be the best story for that individual.
W2575351351.c049.quote: It may be that each person’s story of how she entered into a relationship with God is the best story for that individual.

W2575351351.c050.text: If God eternally knew each person's best story of coming to know God, God would create a world in which each person lives that story.
W2575351351.c050.quote: If God knew this from eternity, then He would do what he could to create a world where each person lives the story of coming to know God that is best for her.

W2575351351.c051.text: Sharing personal testimonies can strengthen and help a religious community flourish by enabling deeper mutual understanding and encouragement.
W2575351351.c051.quote: The community itself is then strengthened as people are able to understand each other in deeper ways. These testimonies may also encourage the members of the community.

W2575351351.c052.text: A testimony that includes nonresistant nonbelief may be especially valuable to its subject and to the subject's religious community.
W2575351351.c052.quote: A testimony which includes a period of nonresistant nonbelief may be particularly valuable.

W2575351351.c053.text: Fictional stories of nonresistant nonbelievers might provide believers with the communal benefits attributed to actual nonresistant nonbelievers.
W2575351351.c053.quote: If W′ contains fictional stories of nonresistant nonbelievers, then the believers in that world might have the communal benefits of those stories;

W2575351351.c054.text: Testimonies from former resistant nonbelievers may be sufficient to secure the testimonial benefits, making nonresistant nonbelief unnecessary.
W2575351351.c054.quote: A second objection is that the stories of resistant nonbelievers would be enough to gain these benefits, so nonresistant nonbelief would not be necessary.

W2575351351.c055.text: The value of former resistant nonbelievers' testimonies does not eliminate the added value of former nonresistant nonbelievers' testimonies.
W2575351351.c055.quote: It does not mean that the testimony of a former nonresistant nonbeliever would not be valuable. That added value is all that is needed to contribute to the MGR.

W2575351351.c056.text: Nonresistant nonbelief may be preferable to resistant nonbelief because nonresistant nonbelievers do not sin through their nonbelief.
W2575351351.c056.quote: Furthermore, nonresistant nonbelief might be a more desirable state of affairs than resistant nonbelief, since nonresistant nonbelievers do not sin in their nonbelief.

W2575351351.c057.text: Testimonies of nonresistant nonbelievers help people appreciate union with God without every person having experienced nonresistant nonbelief.
W2575351351.c057.quote: The personal testimonies of nonresistant nonbelievers allow many people to gain this new appreciation without all of them having been nonresistant nonbelievers themselves.

W2575351351.c058.text: If nobody had been a nonresistant nonbeliever, sharing personal testimonies would plausibly be less common.
W2575351351.c058.quote: Second, if there were never any nonresistant nonbelievers, it’s plausible that the practice of sharing personal testimonies would itself be less common.

W2575351351.c059.text: If nonresistant nonbelief brings about enough goods, a world containing it may be more valuable overall than a world without it.
W2575351351.c059.quote: If there are enough goods brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, then the value of a world containing nonresistant nonbelief might be greater, all else being equal, than the value of a world without nonresistant nonbelief.

W2575351351.c060.text: Any good caused by nonresistant nonbelief contributes to the total value of a world containing nonresistant nonbelief, regardless of how valuable that good is.
W2575351351.c060.quote: A response of this kind simplifies the task of identifying goods because any good brought about by nonresistant nonbelief, no matter how valuable it is, contributes to the value of that world on the whole.

W2575351351.arg1.mp.text: If every identified good can be realized within a relationship with God, the many-goods conditions still hold, so that multiple goods without increased evil, collectively outweighing goods, and no defeat by the accommodation strategy together make the many-goods response succeed.

W2575351351.a1.text: If God were all loving, He would give faultless nonbelievers evidence so they could enter a personal relationship with Him.
W2575351351.a1.quote: If God were all loving, then He would ensure that these people had evidence to believe in Him so that they could enter into a personal relationship with Him.

W2575351351.a2.text: God has sufficient reason to remain hidden if hiddenness makes enough valuable goods sufficiently more valuable.
W2575351351.a2.quote: I argue that if there are valuable goods brought about by God’s hiddenness, then even if each of those goods might obtain without hiddenness, God would have a sufficient reason for remaining hidden so long as enough of those goods would be made sufficiently more valuable because of God’s hiddenness.

W2575351351.a3.text: Nonresistant nonbelievers in the actual world do not entail that God does not exist.
W2575351351.a3.quote: If this is the case, then the existence of ‘nonresistant nonbelievers’ in the actual world does not entail that God does not exist.

W2575351351.arg1.r1.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single bounded episode of nonresistant nonbelief, with its evil measured by the lost relationship over that episode rather than by the number of goods it supports.

W2575351351.arg1.r2.text: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God, after subtracting value shared through common dispositional sources, can collectively make a world containing temporary nonresistant nonbelief more valuable than the lost relationship, which is valued for itself.

W2575351351.arg1.r3.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single bounded episode of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil, provided the goods do not require the episode to be lengthened or intensified beyond what the minimal episode supporting them already involves.

objections.text: Consider Mara, a widow who, through a period of nonresistant nonbelief, becomes unusually attentive to her neighbors. Her absence of belief in God means she does not pray, so she never receives the consolation or moral formation a relationship with God would have given her. Instead she gains three goods: she rebuilds a fractured friendship with her estranged brother, she learns patience through caring for a dying stranger, and she forms a community garden with people who would otherwise have been isolated. Each good is valued below a relationship with God. Yet the collective tally is supposed to exceed that relationship's value. But these three goods are not additive across her life: the friendship and the garden each draw on the same disposition of open-handed attention that a relationship with God would have cultivated more deeply and more reliably. Once the relationship is counted as a standing source of that disposition, the goods are not independent, and the sum she realizes is worth less than the single relationship she forwent.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c017 assumes that individually lesser goods sum additively to exceed a relationship with God, but in Mara's case the goods share a common source whose value is captured by the relationship, so their collective value does not exceed that relationship's value.

objections.text: Mara is a sincere seeker who wants to believe in God but cannot. Consider three goods her nonbelief might produce. First, she shows moral courage by sheltering a refugee without any expectation of divine reward. That needs her nonbelief to last through the crisis, about two months. Second, she comes to deeply understand other doubters. That needs her to feel the full desolation of unanswered searching, which takes a sharper and lonelier phase of doubt, not just mild uncertainty. Third, her brother freely chooses to walk with her through doubt rather than being prompted by evident divine presence. He is slow to choose, so her nonbelief must persist until he does, eighteen months in all. Each good attaches to the same episode of nonbelief, but each requires that episode to be longer or more painful than the previous goods required. Securing all three turns two calm months of doubt into a year and a half of anguish. The goods are not extra fruit from a fixed cost. Each one buys itself by enlarging the evil.
objections.premise_fails_because: c014 fails because when goods depend on the duration or intensity of the nonbelief, adding goods from a single instance of it requires that instance to become longer or more painful, which increases the evil.

objections.text: Mara has never resisted God; she simply lacks belief after years of sincere searching. During a six-month period of nonbelief, she volunteers in a flood shelter and forms a close friendship with Leila, who tells Mara that her kindness kept her alive. This friendship is a genuine good and makes Mara’s life richer. But Mara also spends those months convinced that no loving God is present, grieving alone after her brother’s death and abandoning a community that would have supported her. When she later comes to believe, the friendship remains possible and becomes deeper because Leila joins her in mourning and service. The temporary nonbelief did not make the good sufficiently more valuable: it added loneliness and false despair while contributing nothing that belief could not have supported.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c012 fails because Mara’s temporary nonresistant nonbelief accompanies a good without making that good sufficiently more valuable to overcome the accommodation strategy.

objections.text: Mara sincerely seeks God but remains unconvinced for two years. During that period she develops intellectual courage, patience, and empathy; together these goods barely compensate for the distress and lost relationship caused by her nonbelief. Intellectual courage supplies most of the bundle’s value. Yet Mara could exercise that same courage while believing: God could remain present but let her investigate an ambiguous moral crisis without revealing the answer. She would question her assumptions, risk being wrong, and revise her judgment while retaining the divine relationship. In that accommodated world, she gains equally valuable courage without the distress or relational loss. Patience and empathy alone are too minor to compensate for those harms. Thus accommodating just this one pivotal good removes the only value that made the many-goods package sufficient.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c020 fails because accommodating one individually decisive good can leave the remaining goods unable to justify nonresistant nonbelief.

objections.text: Take Ines, who through temporary nonresistant nonbelief in God's existence lacks any relationship with God. Suppose the goods identified are (a) Ines developing courage in facing uncertainty, (b) her friend Tomas developing compassion by caring for her during her doubt, and (c) a community forming around shared inquiry. The missing premise assumes that because each good could be realized within a relationship with God, the many-goods conditions still hold. But that inference fails here. Within a relationship with God, Ines's courage and Tomas's compassion can be realized without any nonbelief at all, so the nonbelief adds no unique good. The collective-outweighing condition then requires that the nonbelief-dependent goods be realized only through the nonbelief, and that is precisely what the accommodation strategy denies. The premise thus treats 'realizable within a relationship' as if it preserved the conditions that depend on nonbelief being necessary for the goods.
objections.premise_fails_because: The missing premise assumes that the goods being realizable within a relationship with God leaves intact the claim that they require nonresistant nonbelief, when realizability within the relationship removes that necessity and so defeats the many-goods conditions.

objections.text: Belief in God is properly basic. It arises from a faculty that, working as designed, produces it in ordinary circumstances. Nonresistant nonbelief therefore marks that faculty as dulled, and the dulling is itself the evil. Take Maria, raised secular and sincerely open, whose sense of the divine stays silent. Defenders cite three goods from her single case. The first is a freely undertaken search for God, which needs her faculty dulled only until she begins seeking. The second is solidarity with fellow doubters, which needs it dulled through years of shared uncertainty. The third is moral courage without assurance of divine backing, which needs it fully inert at the moment of her ethical crisis, long after her search began. These goods do not share one fixed evil. Each further good requires the malfunction to run longer, reach deeper, or recur at a new point. A truth-aimed faculty failing for longer and more thoroughly is a larger evil. So stacking goods on her nonbelief enlarges the very evil they are meant to offset.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c014 fails because nonresistant nonbelief is a malfunction of a designed belief-forming faculty, and each additional good drawn from it requires extending or deepening that malfunction, which increases the evil.

objections.text: Naturalism holds that goods depend on natural causes and conscious lives, not on an unverified divine relationship. Consider Dana, a committed believer who retains her belief while volunteering at a hospice, studying ecology, reconciling with her estranged sister, and raising a child. These goods arise through ordinary social, psychological, and biological conditions. Her neighbor Eli temporarily becomes nonresistantly nonbelieving and gains the same goods through the same activities, but also suffers needless uncertainty and loss of communal support. If every alleged good is available to Dana without nonbelief, Eli's nonbelief supplies no value-producing cause; it only adds a preventable burden. The many-goods conditions therefore do not still hold merely because the goods can coexist with a relationship with God.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.arg1.mp fails because, by naturalism, goods realizable without nonbelief cannot justify adding nonbelief when it contributes no independent natural benefit.

objections.text: Consider Mara, who sincerely seeks God but remains unable to believe and therefore lacks a relationship with God for ten years. During that period she develops courage, intellectual humility, compassion, and close friendships. Now compare a world in which Mara has an open relationship with God throughout those same ten years while undergoing challenges that produce exactly the same courage, humility, compassion, and friendships. Because every identified good occurs to the same degree in both worlds, nonbelief adds no value in the first world; it only deprives Mara of a valuable relationship. Merely combining several goods does not show that their occurrence alongside nonbelief improves the world when those goods are equally available without that deprivation. The unstated premise fails because realizability within relationship can leave nonbelief contributing only an uncompensated loss, so the many-goods response does not thereby succeed.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise wrongly infers success from the presence and aggregation of goods without showing that nonbelief makes those goods greater or otherwise offsets its distinctive loss.

objections.text: Consider Maren, who for six weeks during a hospital stay has no sense of God's presence and struggles with doubt, while her friend Tobias sits with her nightly. Over those six weeks, Maren learns patience, Tobias deepens his compassion, and the two of them form a bond that persists afterward. Both goods arise from one bounded episode of nonbelief. Measured by the lost relationship over that episode, the evil is six weeks of absent felt presence. But the episode is also the only occasion on which Maren's reliance on Tobias is tested, and her gratitude and his courage are realized only through it. Those goods are not merely two; they are different in kind, and the episode's contribution to them depends on the nonbelief itself, not merely on its duration. Measuring the evil by the lost relationship alone ignores that the same episode enables goods that a relationship with God, which by hypothesis remains intact, would not supply in the same form. The revised premise therefore misidentifies the evil's measure, since the evil it must weigh includes the shape of the goods it makes possible.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 fails because it measures the evil of nonresistant nonbelief solely by the lost relationship over the episode, when the episode's goods depend on the nonbelief in a way that makes the evil's measure partly a function of the goods it enables, so the stated measure does not hold in the Maren and Tobias case.

objections.text: Consider Ana, who loses her felt sense of God for three weeks after her father's death. During this period she grieves honestly, comforts her younger brother, and later becomes a hospice chaplain because the loss taught her to sit with others' unanswered questions. Each of these goods is listed as separate value. But all three flow from one dispositional source: Ana's deep capacity for attentive care, which her ordinary relationship with God had also been expressing. Subtract that shared source, as the revised premise requires, and little residual value remains beyond what the relationship with God, valued for itself, already supplies. The goods were the relationship's own resources redirected, not independent surplus. Summing 'less valuable' goods after subtraction yields a sum that falls short of the lost relationship, which is valued for itself and cannot be recovered by adding instrumental outputs. The aggregation step therefore does not establish that the nonbelief world is more valuable.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise's collective-superiority claim fails because, after subtracting the shared dispositional source, the residual goods in Ana's case sum to less than the intrinsically valued relationship they were drawn from, so aggregation cannot make the nonbelief world more valuable.

objections.text: Consider Mara, who has a bounded two-hour stretch of nonresistant nonbelief on a hiking trail, during which she notices the quiet of the valley and feels a surge of humility. The minimal episode supporting the humility good is just that two-hour stretch. But the episode's minimal form also includes a sustained inner search that the valley's quiet requires: she must stay un-distracted for the full two hours to notice the quiet at all. Her friend Dev, in the same bounded episode, gains a sense of solidarity with strangers at the trailhead, which requires only ten minutes of conversation. Yet to ground that solidarity in the episode, the episode must be extended to include the whole afternoon, since the conversation happens after the hike. The r3 proviso counts 'the minimal episode supporting them' as fixed, but the minimal episode supporting Dev's good is whichever bounded episode contains both the hike and the trailhead talk, which is longer than Mara's minimal episode. Thus the goods' minimal episodes diverge, and the condition that goods not lengthen the episode is either unsatisfiable or quietly relaxed, leaving the stated proviso without a determinate referent.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r3 presupposes a unique minimal bounded episode supporting all the goods, but in the case the goods' minimal supporting episodes differ in length, so the proviso that goods not extend the episode beyond its minimal form cannot be applied determinately.

restatements.plain_english: You cannot count several benefits separately when they mostly come from the same capacity that the lost relationship would have strengthened. restatements.neighboring_tradition: This is a non-additivity and double-counting objection to a theodicy-style outweighing argument: purported compensating goods share a common enabling source that the prevented good would itself supply. The relevant comparison must assess counterfactual dependence and the fuller package of benefits, rather than add overlapping goods as independent items.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges c012 as stated by arguing that temporary nonresistant nonbelief did not make the identified good sufficiently more valuable.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
The objection targets the right premise, but its key move is a counterfactual claim that c012 does not commit to. The argument says temporary nonresistant nonbelief can make a good sufficiently more valuable, and the case you describe is one where the friendship is actually a good that belief could also support. That is compatible with c012 only if the value gained is attributed to nonbelief, not to the good as such. Your case shows that nonbelief adds loneliness and false despair, which are evils, so the net contribution of nonbelief is negative; the good itself is not made more valuable by the nonbelief in your case. I grant this: c012 as worded fails for Mara, because nothing in her six months makes the friendship more valuable than it would have been under belief. The argument therefore needs a restriction: only goods that are unavailable, or substantially altered, under belief count. Temporary nonbelief is required to be the enabling condition of the good, not merely its temporal context. Several of the paper's own resources bear on this: [W2575351351.c046] gives self-sacrifice made possible by nonbelief, where belief would have supplied hope that undercuts the sacrifice, and [W2575351351.c026] requires that the nonbelief be followed by entry into relationship, which Mara's case satisfies. But the self-sacrifice example is the clean case; the friendship case is weaker. The hiddenness literature's own framing, [W2072673546.c003], holds that the existence of nonresistant nonbelief is what matters evidentially, and that framing does not by itself settle whether such nonbelief can yield goods.

Revised premise: A good may overcome the accommodation strategy only if the good is available to the person only through temporary nonresistant nonbelief, so that the nonbelief is its enabling condition and not merely its temporal context.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Mara case is a serious challenge to applying c012 to this particular friendship. On your description, belief would not have prevented the shelter work or friendship, and would have supplied mourning and communal support; so the friendship does not acquire the required extra value through nonbelief. The loneliness and false despair count against, rather than merely alongside, the proposed good.

But that does not refute c012’s conditional possibility claim. It shows that one must establish, case by case, both a good whose value genuinely depends on the temporary nonbelief and a balance sufficient to justify its costs. The author can point to a different proposed mechanism: nonbelief may enable self-sacrifice undertaken without expectation of an afterlife [W2575351351.c046]. And where nonbelief is temporary and later followed by freely entering relationship with God, many goods may outweigh its lost value [W2575351351.c029]. Neither point shows that Mara’s loss is justified; indeed, your account supplies no such differential good. It only leaves open that other temporary cases could satisfy c012 and hence support the many-goods response.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede that Mara’s case does not satisfy c012. Your alternative does not answer why nonbelief itself adds value rather than merely alters a person’s beliefs. Self-sacrifice without expectation of an afterlife may reveal a motive, but belief in an afterlife need not undermine sacrifice, and its absence also removes comfort and support. You must show a value unavailable within relationship with God, not just imagine conduct occurring during nonbelief. Thus c012 remains a bare conditional: if nonbelief made some good sufficiently more valuable, it could be justified. That is true but gives the many-goods response no support until you identify and defend such a differential good.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You are right that merely locating good conduct during nonbelief establishes nothing; Mara shows exactly why. But your stronger requirement—that the good be impossible within relationship with God—is the accommodation criterion c012 is meant to resist. A good may occur in both conditions yet have a value-relevant difference in one. The proposed self-sacrifice case is not simply altered belief: sacrifice made without hope of afterlife can instantiate a distinctive degree of unself-interested relinquishment [W2575351351.c046]. Your point that belief in an afterlife need not undermine sacrifice is fair, but it does not show that it cannot alter the sacrifice’s character or value, nor that the difference could never be sufficient in some temporary case. Mara’s friendship supplies no such difference, so it cannot vindicate the response. Still, c012 is a conditional modal premise, and the self-sacrifice mechanism supplies an identified candidate rather than mere imagination. The argument therefore survives as a claim that the many-goods response may succeed, not as proof that Mara’s nonbelief—or any particular actual case—is justified. Temporary nonbelief followed by relationship with God is also the setting in which lost value may be outweighed by many goods [W2575351351.c029].

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks c014 as stated by arguing that the cited goods cannot arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing the evil, because realizing each additional good requires a longer, deeper, or renewed faculty malfunction.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the evil must be individuated somehow, and that a faculty failing longer and more thoroughly is a larger evil. But c014 does not say the evil is fixed regardless of what the goods require; it says multiple goods may arise without increasing that evil. Your case needs the premise that each good demands a longer, deeper, or later malfunction. That is an empirical and modal claim about Maria's case, and nothing in the three goods you list forces it. A freely undertaken search needs only that she not yet have found God, which is compatible with a faculty that is merely unresponsive at a given time, not dulled. Solidarity with doubters needs shared uncertainty, which can be a feature of the social situation rather than of her faculty. Moral courage without assurance needs the absence of felt divine backing at one moment, which is again a fact about her evidence and not an extension of the malfunction. Compare [W2950222172.a1]: the critic's own worry is that nonresistant nonbelief caused by insufficient evidence counts against God, and your objection, by making the faculty itself the locus of evil, sharpens that worry rather than refuting the many-goods response. [W2780156828.a2] and [W7164197413.a1] both locate the goods in what nonbelief permits, not in extending a defect. So the objection shows that c014 needs an account of how goods are attached to a single episode without multiplying defects. I think the argument survives, provided the author states that the evil of nonresistant nonbelief is the lost relationship and not a per-good dysfunction. That is a clarification, and I do not need a new premise to keep the argument standing against this objection.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You call the evil "the lost relationship" and present that as a mere clarification. It isn't. It quietly drops my premise that belief is properly basic, and you never argued against that premise. If a properly functioning faculty produces belief in ordinary circumstances, then "merely unresponsive at a given time" is not an alternative to dulling. It is the dulling.

Grant your relocation anyway, and my point survives. A relationship lost for fifteen years is a greater loss than one lost for one year. My three goods still need nonbelief at different times: at the start of her search, across years of shared doubt, and at a crisis long afterward. Solidarity with doubters also needs her to be a doubter, so the uncertainty cannot sit only in her social situation.

So c014 holds only if each new good can draw on the same span of nonbelief. You have not shown that any of these three can.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my relocation of the evil to 'the lost relationship' needs defending, and I should not have presented it as a mere clarification. Your premise that belief is properly basic is a substantive commitment the argument does not share, and I concede I have not argued against it. Still, your rejoinder has a gap. Even granting that a properly functioning faculty produces belief in ordinary circumstances, the evil of nonbelief need not scale with the number of goods that nonbelief makes available. The question is whether Maria's three goods require one shared span of nonbelief or three separate ones. You assert the second, but the first good, a freely undertaken search, needs only that the search begin while she has not yet found God, and this is satisfied by the same episode of nonbelief that also supplies the later goods. Solidarity and moral courage can be drawn from that same interval if the interval is the one in which she doubts. Your fifteen-year point shows only that a longer interval is a larger loss, and c014 does not deny that. It says the goods can share the interval. Whether they can is the crux, and I cannot establish it from the case as you describe it. So I concede that c014 does not survive as a bare claim about multiple goods from one instance unless the author adds that the goods are drawn from a single bounded episode of nonbelief, with the evil measured by the lost relationship over that episode.

Revised premise: Multiple goods may arise from a single bounded episode of nonresistant nonbelief, with its evil measured by the lost relationship over that episode rather than by the number of goods it supports.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Maria case identifies an important constraint, but it does not establish that stacking goods always enlarges the evil. You assume that each good must cause a distinct extension or deepening of the faculty’s silence. The defender can instead describe one temporally fixed episode of nonbelief: its already-set duration includes Maria’s search, years of fellowship with doubters, and the later crisis. Those goods can be different consequences of that same profile; counting them separately does not itself make the silence longer, deeper, or recurrent. Nor does the fact that belief might be properly basic entail that every period without it is a progressively worsening malfunction; that is an additional evaluative assumption.

Still, you are right that a many-goods defense cannot simply aggregate goods while silently changing the duration or severity of the nonbelief required for each. It must compare the fixed episode and its alternatives, as the response’s success condition requires [W2575351351.c019]. If the episode is temporary and followed by relationship with God, its lost value may be outweighed by many goods [W2575351351.c029]. Your example defeats only an aggregation that relies on incremental impairment, not the modal claim in [W2575351351.c014].

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You fix the episode's length and then count goods inside it. But a God allowing nonbelief for the sake of goods doesn't find that length given; he sets it. The right comparison is with the shortest silence that secures the first good. Maria's search needs silence only until she begins seeking. Your fixed episode, long enough to reach her later crisis, is longer than that. So relative to the minimal alternative, the further goods are bought with added duration. That is exactly the increase your premise denies.

As for my evaluative assumption, it is only that a longer silence of a truth-aimed faculty is a larger evil. You rely on the same assumption whenever you call the episode "temporary" and weigh it against its alternatives.

I'll narrow my claim. Your premise holds for goods that coincide in time. It fails for goods spread across a life, which are the cases the many-goods response needs.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your revised comparison exposes an ambiguity the premise cannot leave unaddressed. If God could end Maria’s silence once it has secured her search, then retaining it until the later crisis is indeed an additional deprivation relative to that alternative. Calling the whole period one “instance” does not by itself show that its added duration is not added evil; and the defender must accept your evaluative point if the lost relationship is to be weighed at all.

The original premise can still cover genuinely overlapping goods: several consequences may depend on the same necessary period and intensity of nonbelief, so their plurality need not require a further extension. But it cannot simply treat life-spread goods as costless merely because they occur within one biographical episode. The relevant test is comparative: whether the longer profile is the only way to secure the combined goods, or whether alternatives impose greater evil [W2575351351.c019]. If that test is met, temporary nonbelief followed by relationship may still be outweighed [W2575351351.c029]. But c014 as stated does not establish it, and so the argument needs revision.

Revised premise: Multiple goods arising across one person’s nonresistant nonbelief support the many-goods response only if their joint realization requires no more nonbelief-related evil than any available alternative that realizes an adequately comparable set of goods.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges c017 as stated by denying that the individually lesser goods in its example are genuinely additive and collectively more valuable than the forgone relationship with God. It does not attribute a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the tally must be non-double-counted, and the premise c017 does require that the goods' collective value be assessed net of overlap. But Mara's case does not show that overlap is total. The garden and the reconciled friendship are different goods with different recipients: the brother and the isolated neighbors are not benefited merely by a disposition in Mara; they receive goods that a relationship with God would not have supplied to them in the same way. Your objection assumes that the disposition of open-handed attention is the only channel, but the case as described gives Mara a relationship with her brother that the disposition did not produce, and the dying stranger's care is a joint good, not a product of her private cultivation. Schellenberg's own valuation of relationship as intrinsically valuable [W2072673546.c060] cuts against counting the divine relationship as a mere 'standing source' of dispositions: if it is valued for itself, its lost value is not reducible to the attention it would have cultivated, so the comparison is not between a single source and its downstream effects. I also grant that the greater-goods reply is vulnerable where the relationship is treated as infinitely or overwhelmingly valuable [W2575351351.c023, W2950222172.a3], and c028 already concedes that permanent nonbelief may defeat the response. Within the temporary case the argument is only defended as a plausibility claim, and Mara's example, read carefully, shows overlap is partial, not complete. The premise survives, but only with the explicit qualification that the goods be counted net of shared dispositional sources.
rounds.revised_premise: Multiple goods may collectively outweigh a relationship with God only when their value is assessed net of shared dispositional sources, so that each counted good contributes independently to the tally.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You concede that the goods must be counted net of shared dispositional sources, and I accept that as a real gain. But you have not shown that the qualification saves c017 as stated. c017 claims that the goods, individually less valuable than the relationship, collectively make the world more valuable. A net-of-overlap tally is a different claim, and the premise has to be restated to match it.

Your reply also leans on the claim that the brother and the neighbors "receive goods that a relationship with God would not have supplied in the same way." That is true, but it does not answer the overlap. The friendship and the garden still depend on Mara's attentiveness, which is the disposition the relationship would have deepened. You need to show that the attentiveness is not the operative cause of those goods, or that the relationship would not have produced it at the same level. Neither is established by the case.

On intrinsic value: if the relationship is valued for itself, the comparison is with the relationship's own value, not with its dispositional yield. That helps you only if you then grant that the relationship's intrinsic value is not offset by the goods, which is exactly what c017 asserts. You cannot use intrinsic value to escape the overlap and also keep the tally favorable.

So my objection survives in restated form. Restate c017 as a net-of-overlap claim, and show that Mara's goods exceed the relationship after shared sources are subtracted.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my earlier reply conceded too quickly that c017 survives as written. Your restatement point is correct: 'goods collectively make the world more valuable' does not by itself say 'net of overlap,' so the premise must be restated. I accept that. Where I still resist is the claim that Mara's case shows the attentiveness is the operative cause of all three goods. The reconciled friendship with her brother is not obviously a product of a disposition the relationship with God would have deepened; reconciliation often comes from a specific event or a specific choice to call someone, and the case does not say the relationship with God would have produced it. Likewise the dying stranger's care is shared with the stranger, who is a recipient of the good, not merely a channel. So overlap is at most partial, and your demand that I show it is zero is stronger than what the objection needs to defeat c017. Your intrinsic-value point is the stronger one: if the relationship is valued for itself [W2072673546.c060], then its loss cannot be offset by a dispositional yield, and the comparison is between goods and the relationship's own value. I grant that this does not by itself make the tally favorable. The honest position is that the many-goods response needs an explicit net-of-overlap restatement and an independent argument that the surviving non-overlapping goods, taken together, exceed a relationship valued for itself. The case as described establishes neither. Schellenberg-style plausibility is not enough here, and the greater-goods reply is exposed to the concern that a relationship valued intrinsically resists being outweighed [W2950222172.a3, W2575351351.c023].

Revised premise: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God, after subtracting value shared through common dispositional sources, can collectively make a world containing temporary nonresistant nonbelief more valuable than the lost relationship, which is valued for itself.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: Your Mara case identifies a real constraint: one cannot simply count three outcomes alongside a relationship with God if the relationship would already secure the same outcomes, or their common source, more fully. Schellenberg’s point that relationship is intrinsically valuable must also be retained in the comparison [W2072673546.c060]. But that shows at most that Mara’s stipulated package has not yet established the premise; it does not refute its modal claim [W2575351351.c017]. The relevant comparison is between whole feasible histories, not a tally of separately named goods. That a divine relationship cultivates open-handed attention does not entail that it would produce this reconciliation, this care relation, and this cooperative garden together, with their particular interpersonal histories. Nor does the availability of each good within relationship establish that the entire package is available there without loss; this is precisely why individual accommodation does not automatically defeat the many-goods strategy. Some goods may also depend on believers and wider social relations rather than merely on Mara’s disposition [W2575351351.c041]. If, however, your stronger counterfactual is true—God-relationship reliably yields all three goods at least as well—then Mara’s episode supplies no many-goods justification. The argument survives only as a possibility claim, especially for bounded temporary nonbelief whose lost relationship-value can be outweighed [W2575351351.c029].

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You are right that my case, as stated, does not show the modal claim false. Mara's package does not establish that a divine relationship would yield these three goods, with their particular histories, at least as well. But your reply leaves my central point standing. The claim in c017 is that the goods' collective value exceeds the relationship's value. That requires the goods to be summable, and you have not said why they are. Two of Mara's goods draw on the same disposition of open-handed attention. If that overlap holds, her realized value is not the sum of three independent contributions, and the tally overcounts.

Your fallback to a possibility claim does not avoid this. A possibility claim about bounded nonbelief still needs a case where the goods are non-overlapping and collectively outweigh. Mara does not supply one, so the revised premise cannot be defended by appeal to her.

I accept that c017 survives only if restricted to goods that are independent of any shared source the relationship would also provide. Please state that restriction in c017 and identify a case that meets it. Without that, the collective-value claim is unsupported.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that Mara, as described, cannot bear the weight placed on her: the friendship and garden partly instantiate the same attention, so treating them as three fully separate increments overcounts. Nor can I answer that by merely relabeling the claim modal. A bounded episode still needs a non-duplicative package whose net value exceeds the episode’s lost relationship-value. Temporary nonbelief remains the relevant setting, since its loss may be outweighed, unlike permanent nonbelief [W2575351351.c029].

The smallest repair is not your stronger requirement that goods have no shared source at all. Distinct goods may share a source and still add value; what matters is that their value is not already included in, or guaranteed by, the God-relationship alternative. A candidate case would involve a bounded episode enabling three irreducible relations: reconciliation with an estranged brother, a particular reciprocal care relation with a dying stranger, and an enduring mutual-support network among isolated neighbors. Their common occasion may be Mara’s situation, but the relevant comparison must establish that a relationship with God would not secure that whole relational package without foreclosing its distinctive value. The thought that some relevant goods may require other believers and broader social relations supports this non-individual comparison [W2575351351.c041].

So Mara is not a successful instance of c017 as stated. The argument survives only with the revised premise below; absent evidence of such a package, its conclusion is a live possibility rather than an established justification.

Revised premise: Goods each less valuable than a relationship with God can collectively make a world containing a bounded episode of nonresistant nonbelief more valuable only when their jointly realized net value is not duplicated or guaranteed by the available God-relationship alternative and exceeds that episode’s lost relationship-value.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the episode's length and pain matter, and that c014 as worded is too quick: if each good requires a longer or sharper episode, then the goods are not free riders on one fixed cost, and c014's 'without increasing that evil' fails for Mara's case. But the argument's own framing, via arg1.r1, locates the evil in the lost relationship over the episode, so the question is whether Mara's extended doubt lengthens that loss. It does: two months versus eighteen months is a larger lost relationship, so the stated evil does rise with the goods' demands. The defender's best reply is that the many-goods response need not claim that goods are free; it needs only that the goods' combined value exceeds the increase in lost relationship. Your case shows that for goods requiring escalating duration, that comparison must be made explicitly, not assumed. Greater goods of this kind are the sort the hiddenness literature treats as possibly unknown rather than guaranteed [W2072673546.c089]. Whether they can cover the additional evil is an empirical-style weighing the argument has not yet done. I therefore concede that c014, as unrestricted, does not survive; the argument survives only with the restricted premise below.

rounds.content:
You concede that Mara's goods enlarge the evil, but retreat to bare possibility: some episode might be "independently fixed," with several goods arising inside it. I ask what fixes it. A perfectly loving God permits nonbelief only for the sake of goods, so the episode's length and severity must be set by the goods themselves, specifically by the most demanding one. The other goods ride free only if they need no more than that episode already supplies. But then the episode is justified mainly by its most demanding good, and the "many" add only what fits inside its shadow.

It is between the loss of the maximally demanding warranted episode and the goods genuinely realized within that episode without requiring any further loss. Your point does not falsify c014’s existential claim: several goods may still arise during one bounded episode without extending or intensifying it [W2575351351.c014]. Nor does it undermine the temporary-nonbelief framework: relationship can follow such an episode [W2575351351.c026], and its loss may in principle be outweighed [W2575351351.c029]. objection.text: Consider Mara, a widow who, through a period of nonresistant nonbelief, becomes unusually attentive to her neighbors. Her absence of belief in God means she does not pray, so she never receives the consolation or moral formation a relationship with God would have given her. Instead she gains three goods: she rebuilds a fractured friendship with her estranged brother, she learns patience through caring for a dying stranger, and she forms a community garden with people who would otherwise have been isolated. Each good is valued below a relationship with God. Yet the collective tally is supposed to exceed that relationship's value. But these three goods are not additive across her life: the friendship and the garden each draw on the same disposition of open-handed attention that a relationship with God would have cultivated more deeply and more reliably. Once the relationship is counted as a standing source of that disposition, the goods are not independent, and the sum she realizes is worth less than the single relationship she forwent.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c017 assumes that individually lesser goods sum additively to exceed a relationship with God, but in Mara's case the goods share a common source whose value is captured by the relationship, so their collective value does not exceed that relationship's value.

objection.text: Mara is a sincere seeker who wants to believe in God but cannot. Consider three goods her nonbelief might produce. First, she shows moral courage by sheltering a refugee without any expectation of divine reward. That needs her nonbelief to last through the crisis, about two months. Second, she comes to deeply understand other doubters. That needs her to feel the full desolation of unanswered searching, which takes a sharper and lonelier phase of doubt, not just mild uncertainty. Third, her brother freely chooses to walk with her through doubt rather than being prompted by evident divine presence. He is slow to choose, so her nonbelief must persist until he does, eighteen months in all. Each good attaches to the same episode of nonbelief, but each requires that episode to be longer or more painful than the previous goods required. Securing all three turns two calm months of doubt into a year and a half of anguish. The goods are not extra fruit from a fixed cost. Each one buys itself by enlarging the evil.
objection.premise_fails_because: c014 fails because when goods depend on the duration or intensity of the nonbelief, adding goods from a single instance of it requires that instance to become longer or more painful, which increases the evil.

objection.text: Mara has never resisted God; she simply lacks belief after years of sincere searching. During a six-month period of nonbelief, she volunteers in a flood shelter and forms a close friendship with Leila, who tells Mara that her kindness kept her alive. This friendship is a genuine good and makes Mara’s life richer. But Mara also spends those months convinced that no loving God is present, grieving alone after her brother’s death and abandoning a community that would have supported her. When she later comes to believe, the friendship remains possible and becomes deeper because Leila joins her in mourning and service. The temporary nonbelief did not make the good sufficiently more valuable: it added loneliness and false despair while contributing nothing that belief could not have supported.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c012 fails because Mara’s temporary nonresistant nonbelief accompanies a good without making that good sufficiently more valuable to overcome the accommodation strategy.

objection.text: Mara sincerely seeks God but remains unconvinced for two years. During that period she develops intellectual courage, patience, and empathy; together these goods barely compensate for the distress and lost relationship caused by her nonbelief. Intellectual courage supplies most of the bundle’s value. Yet Mara could exercise that same courage while believing: God could remain present but let her investigate an ambiguous moral crisis without revealing the answer. She would question her assumptions, risk being wrong, and revise her judgment while retaining the divine relationship. In that accommodated world, she gains equally valuable courage without the distress or relational loss. Patience and empathy alone are too minor to compensate for those harms. Thus accommodating just this one pivotal good removes the only value that made the many-goods package sufficient.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c020 fails because accommodating one individually decisive good can leave the remaining goods unable to justify nonresistant nonbelief.

objection.text: Take Ines, who through temporary nonresistant nonbelief in God's existence lacks any relationship with God. Suppose the goods identified are (a) Ines developing courage in facing uncertainty, (b) her friend Tomas developing compassion by caring for her during her doubt, and (c) a community forming around shared inquiry. The missing premise assumes that because each good could be realized within a relationship with God, the many-goods conditions still hold. But that inference fails here. Within a relationship with God, Ines's courage and Tomas's compassion can be realized without any nonbelief at all, so the nonbelief adds no unique good. The collective-outweighing condition then requires that the nonbelief-dependent goods be realized only through the nonbelief, and that is precisely what the accommodation strategy denies. The premise thus treats 'realizable within a relationship' as if it preserved the conditions that depend on nonbelief being necessary for the goods.
objection.premise_fails_because: The missing premise assumes that the goods being realizable within a relationship with God leaves intact the claim that they require nonresistant nonbelief, when realizability within the relationship removes that necessity and so defeats the many-goods conditions.

objection.text: Belief in God is properly basic. It arises from a faculty that, working as designed, produces it in ordinary circumstances. Nonresistant nonbelief therefore marks that faculty as dulled, and the dulling is itself the evil. Take Maria, raised secular and sincerely open, whose sense of the divine stays silent. Defenders cite three goods from her single case. The first is a freely undertaken search for God, which needs her faculty dulled only until she begins seeking. The second is solidarity with fellow doubters, which needs it dulled through years of shared uncertainty. The third is moral courage without assurance of divine backing, which needs it fully inert at the moment of her ethical crisis, long after her search began. These goods do not share one fixed evil. Each further good requires the malfunction to run longer, reach deeper, or recur at a new point. A truth-aimed faculty failing for longer and more thoroughly is a larger evil. So stacking goods on her nonbelief enlarges the very evil they are meant to offset.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.c014 fails because nonresistant nonbelief is a malfunction of a designed belief-forming faculty, and each additional good drawn from it requires extending or deepening that malfunction, which increases the evil.

objection.text: Naturalism holds that goods depend on natural causes and conscious lives, not on an unverified divine relationship. Consider Dana, a committed believer who retains her belief while volunteering at a hospice, studying ecology, reconciling with her estranged sister, and raising a child. These goods arise through ordinary social, psychological, and biological conditions. Her neighbor Eli temporarily becomes nonresistantly nonbelieving and gains the same goods through the same activities, but also suffers needless uncertainty and loss of communal support. If every alleged good is available to Dana without nonbelief, Eli's nonbelief supplies no value-producing cause; it only adds a preventable burden. The many-goods conditions therefore do not still hold merely because the goods can coexist with a relationship with God.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2575351351.arg1.mp fails because, by naturalism, goods realizable without nonbelief cannot justify adding nonbelief when it contributes no independent natural benefit.

objection.text: Consider Mara, who sincerely seeks God but remains unable to believe and therefore lacks a relationship with God for ten years. During that period she develops courage, intellectual humility, compassion, and close friendships. Now compare a world in which Mara has an open relationship with God throughout those same ten years while undergoing challenges that produce exactly the same courage, humility, compassion, and friendships. Because every identified good occurs to the same degree in both worlds, nonbelief adds no value in the first world; it only deprives Mara of a valuable relationship. Merely combining several goods does not show that their occurrence alongside nonbelief improves the world when those goods are equally available without that deprivation. The unstated premise fails because realizability within relationship can leave nonbelief contributing only an uncompensated loss, so the many-goods response does not thereby succeed.
objection.premise_fails_because: The premise wrongly infers success from the presence and aggregation of goods without showing that nonbelief makes those goods greater or otherwise offsets its distinctive loss.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
The objection targets the right premise, but its key move is a counterfactual claim that c012 does not commit to. The argument says temporary nonresistant nonbelief can make a good sufficiently more valuable, and the case you describe is one where the friendship is actually a good that belief could also support. That is compatible with c012 only if the value gained is attributed to nonbelief, not to the good as such. Your case shows that nonbelief adds loneliness and false despair, which are evils, so the net contribution of nonbelief is negative; the good itself is not made more valuable by the nonbelief in your case. I grant this: c012 as worded fails for Mara, because nothing in her six months makes the friendship more valuable than it would have been under belief. The argument therefore needs a restriction: only goods that are unavailable, or substantially altered, under belief count. Temporary nonbelief is required to be the enabling condition of the good, not merely its temporal context. Several of the paper's own resources bear on this: [W2575351351.c046] gives self-sacrifice made possible by nonbelief, where belief would have supplied hope that undercuts the sacrifice, and [W2575351351.c026] requires that the nonbelief be followed by entry into relationship, which Mara's case satisfies. But the self-sacrifice example is the clean case; the friendship case is weaker. The hiddenness literature's own framing, [W2072673546.c003], holds that the existence of nonresistant nonbelief is what matters evidentially, and that framing does not by itself settle whether such nonbelief can yield goods.

Revised premise: A good may overcome the accommodation strategy only if the good is available to the person only through temporary nonresistant nonbelief, so that the nonbelief is its enabling condition and not merely its temporal context.

Your Mara case is a serious challenge to applying c012 to this particular friendship. The loneliness and false despair count against, rather than merely alongside, the proposed good.

But that does not refute c012’s conditional possibility claim. It shows that one must establish, case by case, both a good whose value genuinely depends on the temporary nonbelief and a balance sufficient to justify its costs. The author can point to a different proposed mechanism: nonbelief may enable self-sacrifice undertaken without expectation of an afterlife [W2575351351.c046]. And where nonbelief is temporary and later followed by freely entering relationship with God, many goods may outweigh its lost value [W2575351351.c029]. Neither point shows that Mara’s loss is justified; indeed, your account supplies no such differential good. It only leaves open that other temporary cases could satisfy c012 and hence support the many-goods response.

turn.content: You concede that Mara’s case does not satisfy c012. Your alternative does not answer why nonbelief itself adds value rather than merely alters a person’s beliefs. Self-sacrifice without expectation of an afterlife may reveal a motive, but belief in an afterlife need not undermine sacrifice, and its absence also removes comfort and support. You must show a value unavailable within relationship with God, not just imagine conduct occurring during nonbelief. Thus c012 remains a bare conditional: if nonbelief made some good sufficiently more valuable, it could be justified. That is true but gives the many-goods response no support until you identify and defend such a differential good.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content: You are right that merely locating good conduct during nonbelief establishes nothing; Mara shows exactly why. But your stronger requirement—that the good be impossible within relationship with God—is the accommodation criterion c012 is meant to resist. A good may occur in both conditions yet have a value-relevant difference in one. The proposed self-sacrifice case is not simply altered belief: sacrifice made without hope of afterlife can instantiate a distinctive degree of unself-interested relinquishment [W2575351351.c046]. Your point that belief in an afterlife need not undermine sacrifice is fair, but it does not show that it cannot alter the sacrifice’s character or value, nor that the difference could never be sufficient in some temporary case. Mara’s friendship supplies no such difference, so it cannot vindicate the response. Still, c012 is a conditional modal premise, and the self-sacrifice mechanism supplies an identified candidate rather than mere imagination. The argument therefore survives as a claim that the many-goods response may succeed, not as proof that Mara’s nonbelief—or any particular actual case—is justified. Temporary nonbelief followed by relationship with God is also the setting in which lost value may be outweighed by many goods [W2575351351.c029].

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that the evil must be individuated somehow, and that a faculty failing longer and more thoroughly is a larger evil. But c014 does not say the evil is fixed regardless of what the goods require; it says multiple goods may arise without increasing that evil. Your case needs the premise that each good demands a longer, deeper, or later malfunction. That is an empirical and modal claim about Maria's case, and nothing in the three goods you list forces it. A freely undertaken search needs only that she not yet have found God, which is compatible with a faculty that is merely unresponsive at a given time, not dulled. Solidarity with doubters needs shared uncertainty, which can be a feature of the social situation rather than of her faculty. Moral courage without assurance needs the absence of felt divine backing at one moment, which is again a fact about her evidence and not an extension of the malfunction. Compare [W2950222172.a1]: the critic's own worry is that nonresistant nonbelief caused by insufficient evidence counts against God, and your objection, by making the faculty itself the locus of evil, sharpens that worry rather than refuting the many-goods response. [W2780156828.a2] and [W7164197413.a1] both locate the goods in what nonbelief permits, not in extending a defect. So the objection shows that c014 needs an account of how goods are attached to a single episode without multiplying defects. I think the argument survives, provided the author states that the evil of nonresistant nonbelief is the lost relationship and not a per-good dysfunction. That is a clarification, and I do not need a new premise to keep the argument standing against this objection.

turn.content:
You call the evil "the lost relationship" and present that as a mere clarification. It isn't. It quietly drops my premise that belief is properly basic, and you never argued against that premise. If a properly functioning faculty produces belief in ordinary circumstances, then "merely unresponsive at a given time" is not an alternative to dulling. It is the dulling.

Grant your relocation anyway, and my point survives. A relationship lost for fifteen years is a greater loss than one lost for one year. My three goods still need nonbelief at different times: at the start of her search, across years of shared doubt, and at a crisis long afterward. Solidarity with doubters also needs her to be a doubter, so the uncertainty cannot sit only in her social situation.

So c014 holds only if each new good can draw on the same span of nonbelief. You have not shown that any of these three can.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that my relocation of the evil to 'the lost relationship' needs defending, and I should not have presented it as a mere clarification. Your premise that belief is properly basic is a substantive commitment the argument does not share, and I concede I have not argued against it. Still, your rejoinder has a gap. Even granting that a properly functioning faculty produces belief in ordinary circumstances, the evil of nonbelief need not scale with the number of goods that nonbelief makes available. The question is whether Maria's three goods require one shared span of nonbelief or three separate ones. You assert the second, but the first good, a freely undertaken search, needs only that the search begin while she has not yet found God, and this is satisfied by the same episode of nonbelief that also supplies the later goods. Your fifteen-year point shows only that a longer interval is a larger loss, and c014 does not deny that. It says the goods can share the interval.
